title: Morse started by laying the wire underground between Washington and Baltimore, using a plough built
description:
Morse started by laying the wire underground between Washington and Baltimore, using a plough built by Ezra Cornell. After about nine and a half miles, the line was failing. A partner had bought wire with defective insulation.

Out of time, Morse took Cornell's advice and strung the wire overhead instead. Cooke and Wheatstone were already using poles in England.

chestnut poles, about 300 feet apart, that replaced the buried pipe in the spring of 1844.

On 1 May 1844, before the line was finished, it carried news of Henry Clay's nomination for president. 'What hath God wrought', sent on 24 May, was the official opening, not the first message.

The phrase was not even Morse's choice. It was suggested by Annie Ellsworth, from the Book of Numbers. It arrived in Baltimore as dents in a moving strip of paper, not as sound.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore%E2%80%93Washington_telegraph_line: confirms Congress appropriated $30,000 in March 1843 for the line; that Morse first laid the wire underground using Ezra Cornell's plough, starting 21 October 1843, and stopped after about 9.5 miles because the line was failing; that he switched to overhead wire on about 700 chestnut poles from 1 April 1844; that on 1 May 1844 the unfinished line carried news of the Whig Party's nomination of Henry Clay; that 'What hath God wrought' was sent on 24 May 1844 from the Capitol to Alfred Vail in Baltimore, the phrase suggested by Annie Ellsworth; and that the Postmaster General judged the line unlikely ever to earn income, returning it to private development.
- https://www.loc.gov/static/collections/samuel-morse-papers/articles-and-essays/invention-of-the-telegraph/: the Library of Congress confirms the underground wire failed because a partner, Congressman F. O. J. Smith, bought wire with defective insulation; that Cornell suggested stringing wire overhead; and that Morse's receiver recorded messages as dents in a moving paper tape.
